items.title: Mississippi elects Democrat Colom as state's first post-Civil War Black senator
items.standfirst: Democratic nominee Scott Colom defeated Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith on Wednesday in Mississippi's closely contested US Senate race after a prolonged ballot counting process, giving the state its first Black US senator since post-Civil War Reconstruction. Colom's narrow victory is a seismic shift in Mississippi, which has been controlled mostly by white conservatives for generations despite having the largest share of Black residents of any US state.

items.title: Scott Colom Wins Nail-Biter Mississippi Race, Becoming State’s First Democratic Senator-Elect Since 1982
items.standfirst: Colom defeated incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith to become the first Democrat elected to the Senate from Mississippi since 1982.
items.content: Mississippi Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate Scott Colom speaks during a campaign rally in Tupelo on Oct. 30, 2026. —Brad Vest—Getty ImagesDemocratic challenger Scott Colom has defeated incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in what was one of the tightest races of the 2026 midterms, marking another stunning victory for his party. The Associated Press called the race on Wednesday, more than a week after Election Day.Colom, a district attorney for Mississippi’s 16th Judicial District, becomes the first Black Senator elected in the state since 1874 and the first Democratic Senator elected there since 1982. Trump won Mississippi in the 2024 presidential election by nearly 23 points.Read More: The Democratic Wins No Election Forecaster ExpectedColom’s victory marks the eighth Republican-held Senate seat Democrats have flipped in this year’s midterms, securing a majority of at least 55 seats, including independents who caucus with the party. They will nevertheless remain short of the 60 votes generally needed to overcome a filibuster on legislation.“I make a solemn commitment to each and every Mississippian tonight,” Colom said at a victory rally at Tougaloo College on Wednesday night. “In every decision I make, I will never forget that the most important thing is: Mississippi matters.”Colom’s margin of victory was narrow: he had 49.2% of the vote to Hyde-Smith’s 48.7%, with an estimated 99% of ballots counted, according to the AP. Mississippi law provides for neither automatic nor candidate-requested recounts, though a court can order one.“There were times,” Colom said during his victory speech, “when I couldn’t get donors to answer the phone, they didn’t believe a moment like this was possible, but I kept the faith. … There are so many people that had faith in Mississippi at times where it seemed impossible.”“While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters,” Hyde-Smith said in a two-minute concession speech. “I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state.”A spokesperson for Hyde-Smith said she called Colom to concede before the video was posted. At the end of the call, Colom reportedly said, “God bless you and thank you, Senator.”There are certain paths that a losing candidate can pursue, however, according to a blog post from Derek Muller, a professor and expert on election law at the University of Notre Dame. For one, Muller wrote, they could mount a legal challenge over decisions to include or leave out certain ballots in the count, for instance. Or they could appeal to the U.S. Senate to determine who should be seated in the chamber.The Mississippi race remained too close to call for days after the election, with the two candidates split by only a razor-thin margin of as low as 0.1% with more than 95% of votes counted. Counting took longer because county election officials had to individually review affidavit ballots—provisional votes cast when a voter’s eligibility or identification needed further verification.“Over the past week, our campaign has worked tirelessly to ensure every legally cast vote was counted, and that the people of Mississippi received a fair and transparent election,” Hyde-Smith said.Both candidates expressed confidence that they would win leading up to the final vote count. Colom in a statement said he was “confident we will ultimately flip this seat,” while Hyde-Smith told her constituents, “I assure you, I will continue to be your U.S. Senator.”Ahead of Election Day, the Senate race was filled with name-calling and tit-for-tat jabs over the candidates’ differing ideologies. Colom called Hyde-Smith a “chicken” for refusing to debate, something she hasn’t done since 2018. In response, Hyde-Smith’s campaign defended her by saying that there was “no point in debating someone so out of touch with Mississippi that he advocates for the sex change surgeries for children,” referencing Colom’s stance on gender-affirming care. Colom, whom Hyde-Smith called “the most radical liberal” to run for office in Mississippi, in 2021 signed a letter opposing the criminalization of transgender people and gender-affirming care, but has said that he opposes gender-affirming surgeries for minors. Hyde-Smith has similarly sought to paint Colom in a negative light by labeling him a “Transgender Defender” throughout her campaign. Colom created a nickname of his own for his opponent, referring to Hyde-Smith as “Cindy High Prices.” Colom, whose campaign focused in part on lowering consumer prices, criticized the Republican incumbent for comments that appeared to brush off concerns about rising beef prices in particular, zoning in on a February television interview in which the Mississippi Senator said in response to a question about rising costs for beef and other food that there were “so many proteins to choose from.” Colom’s campaign put out a viral ad that suggested that voters, instead of picking another protein, should “pick another Senator.” The jab against Hyde-Smith was also made in reference to her support for Trump, whose approval ratings have sunk to new lows in large part due to mounting dissatisfaction with his handling of the economy. Hyde-Smith last month called Trump “the best President of our lifetime” during a rally where both Republicans shared the stageIn an unorthodox strategy, Colom attended Trump’s rally in Mississippi in an attempt to talk to voters about key issues and later said he had converted some of those he spoke to.“I’m gonna show up and I’m gonna listen, and when on Nov. 3 we pick a new United States Senator, I’m gonna represent them a lot better,” he said on Oct. 26.The two candidates were at odds on other key policy issues as well. Hyde-Smith, who chairs the Senate Pro-Life Caucus, also levied accusations against Colom for his position on abortion. Colom has described himself as pro-life, while saying that he trusts that women will “make the choices that are best for them.”When it comes to the war in Iran, meanwhile, Colom has opposed the conflict and its effect in driving up costs. Hyde-Smith has for her part acknowledged the war’s impact on the economy, but said it was necessary for national security.She also supported Trump’s “Big Beautiful Bill” and cuts to Medicaid, which Colom has said he hopes to help reverse if elected.The candidates have a history predating their tight Senate race as well. In 2023, Hyde-Smith blocked Colom from a federal judgeship after he was tapped for the position by President Joe Biden, citing Colom's support for transgender rights, among other issues.

items.title: Mississippi elects Democrat Scott Colom to Senate in massive upset
items.standfirst: Colom's win is a boost to the Democratic Party as it seeks to gain a larger foothold in the South.
items.content: Mississippi voted blue, in a shock win for Democrats.Democrat Scott Colom ousted Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in a state that went for President Donald Trump by 23 points in 2024. He will be the first Black senator elected in Mississippi since the Reconstruction era — and the first Democrat from the state headed to the Senate in 44 years.Colom, a Democratic district attorney, ran a scrappy campaign that saw some national money and resources in the final stretch of the race.Hyde-Smith was appointed to the Senate in 2018 and had since won election to the seat twice, but she faced attacks from Colom that she was out of touch and indifferent to rising grocery and gas prices during Trump’s second term.National Democratic groups hadn't paid much attention to the Mississippi Senate race until an October surge of excitement for Colom drew late spending and attention.Colom's win is a boost to the Democratic Party as it seeks to gain a larger foothold in the South and improve their standing with Black voters. It’s also a major vindication for Colom and other Southern Democrats who argued Mississippi had been neglected for far too long.

items.title: House Republicans Block Hegseth Impeachment, but Democrats Could Revive Effort in January
items.standfirst: The House voted 211-204 to defeat a resolution brought by Rep. Thomas Massie
items.content: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is seen at the White House on Oct. 29, 2026 in Washington, DC. —Finn Gomez—Getty ImagesThe Republican-led House on Tuesday narrowly rejected a push to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over unauthorized military hostilities in Iran, Venezuela and Yemen, shielding one of President Donald Trump's closest allies from an immediate reckoning but setting the stage for a renewed confrontation when Democrats take control of Congress in January.The House voted 211-204 to defeat a resolution brought by Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, a Republican who has repeatedly clashed with Trump, preventing lawmakers from considering eight articles of impeachment accusing Hegseth of violating the Constitution, conducting unauthorized military operations, and abusing the powers of his office.The vote offered a temporary reprieve for Hegseth, who has faced mounting criticism over the administration's conduct of the Iran war, and demonstrated Trump's continued hold over congressional Republicans despite the party's sweeping losses in last week's midterm elections. But it may have only delayed a political showdown over the defense secretary's future. Democrats, who won control of both chambers of Congress in the election, will have an opportunity to revive the impeachment effort when the new Congress convenes on Jan. 3, potentially making Hegseth the third Cabinet member in American history to be impeached.With a Democratic majority in the House, impeachment articles would stand a substantially greater chance of passage. Unlike a Senate conviction, which requires support of a two-thirds majority, impeachment in the House requires only a simple majority. Democrats could therefore approve articles without Republican support if enough of their members backed the effort.Such a vote would make Hegseth only the third Cabinet secretary in American history to be impeached, following William Belknap, President Ulysses S. Grant's secretary of war, in 1876, and Alejandro Mayorkas, President Joe Biden's homeland security secretary, in 2024. It would also raise the prospect of a Senate trial soon after Democrats take control of the chamber, forcing lawmakers in both parties to confront allegations of unlawful military conduct at a time when the Iran war has become a major political liability for the White House.The current impeachment effort was led by Massie, who lost his Republican primary this year to a candidate backed by Trump. Massie introduced the eight articles on Monday, arguing that Hegseth had repeatedly exceeded his legal authority in directing military operations and disregarded congressional restrictions on the use of force. “We’re not indicting him for being bad at his job,” Massie said Monday. “The argument here is that he’s broken laws and he’s violated the Constitution.”Hegseth has rejected the allegations as politically motivated and insisted that he has no intention of resigning. At a news conference Tuesday morning, he dismissed the impeachment effort as the work of a “disgruntled and defeated congressman.” His spokesman, Sean Parnell, said the Pentagon had acted lawfully and that Hegseth intended to remain in office through the end of Trump's term.Trump has stood firmly behind his defense secretary, even as the war has fueled public frustration and deepened divisions within his party. Asked whether he would continue supporting Hegseth if the House impeached him, the president replied, “Yeah I’ll stand by him.” In a social-media post Monday night, he urged lawmakers to defend Hegseth: “Congress, stand up for Pete!!!”While Tuesday's vote failed, the political circumstances surrounding the effort are poised to change dramatically. In the new year, Democrats will have the power to set the House's agenda, conduct investigations, and bring impeachment resolutions to the floor without relying on Republican defections to overcome procedural obstacles.The eight articles introduced by Massie encompassed some of the administration's most controversial military decisions, from the war in Iran to its operations in Venezuela and strikes against suspected drug traffickers in the Caribbean and Pacific.Three focused on Iran, accusing Hegseth of helping initiate the conflict without congressional authorization, continuing military operations despite congressional demands to end the war or obtain approval for it, and violating statutory deadlines for withdrawing American forces from unauthorized hostilities.The charges invoked the War Powers Resolution of 1973, which limits the president's ability to conduct prolonged military operations without congressional approval. The Trump administration has maintained that the president possesses the constitutional authority as commander in chief to direct the campaign, a position that has brought the White House into conflict with lawmakers who argue that Congress has been unlawfully sidelined.Other articles accuse Hegseth of overseeing unlawful strikes against boats suspected of carrying drugs, failing to adequately protect civilians during military operations and directing the January mission that captured Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife, which Massie argues constituted an act of war. Another challenges the administration's 2025 campaign against Houthi forces in Yemen, which drew scrutiny after senior officials discussed planned strikes in a Signal group chat that inadvertently included a journalist.A separate charge accuses Hegseth of retaliating against Sen. Mark Kelly, an Arizona Democrat and retired Navy captain, after Kelly participated in a video reminding service members that they were not obligated to follow illegal orders. Hegseth censured Kelly and initiated disciplinary proceedings that threatened his military rank and pension. A federal judge subsequently blocked the punishment, though the Justice Department has appealed.Together, the articles sought to establish a pattern of alleged misconduct extending beyond the Iran war, challenging the administration's expansive interpretation of executive authority and its willingness to use military force without congressional approval.Hegseth and his allies have portrayed the allegations as an attack on successful military operations. Speaking Monday, Hegseth suggested that seeking his removal over the Iran war, the strikes against suspected drug traffickers and the capture of Maduro amounted to “taking issue with the troops and what they accomplished.”Trump offered a similar defense Sunday, saying Hegseth was “guilty of two things, basically winning two wars.”While some of the party’s base are pushing for a Trump impeachment, several senior Democrats have told TIME that targeting the defense secretary would offer Congress a more attainable means of challenging the administration's conduct of the war. "There are Republicans who would support impeaching Hegseth who might not support doing it to Trump," says Rep. Adam Smith of Washington, who is in line to chair the House Armed Services Committee. Democrats have also not ruled out impeaching other members of Trump’s cabinet, including Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. “Impeachment of Pete Hegseth or Robert F. Kennedy Jr. or anyone in the cabinet presents a completely different set of political considerations than the president,” says Rep. Jamie Raskin of Maryland, an impeachment manager in Trump’s first term who is in line to chair the Judiciary Committee.

items.title: Hegseth Could Be the Third Cabinet Secretary Impeached in U.S. History
items.standfirst: House Republicans blocked Hegseth’s impeachment, but Democrats could revive the effort when they take control of Congress in January.
items.content: Secretary of War Pete Hegseth speaks during a news conference at the Pentagon on Nov. 10, 2026. —Chip Somodevilla––Getty ImagesDefense Secretary Pete Hegseth narrowly escaped an impeachment attempt Tuesday after the Republican-led House rejected a resolution filed by a GOP lawmaker.While Hegseth has been granted a reprieve, it's possible the Democrats could revive the effort in January, when they take control of both the House and Senate following sweeping victories in the midterms. The House voted 211-204 to defeat the measure reintroduced Monday by Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky. The eight articles of impeachment accused Hegseth of violating the War Powers Resolution of 1973, citing the lack of congressional oversight on the Iran war which Massie argued was “unlawful from its inception.” Another charge accused Hegseth of “ignoring laws that minimize civilian casualties.” The charges also alleged the “kidnapping of a sovereign foreign leader,” in reference to the U.S.’ capture of former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in January.Hegseth dismissed the impeachment effort as a “political spectacle,” referring to the resolutions put forward by Massie, who lost the Republican primary in May to a Trump-backed challenger, as a “farce” that “mock the Constitution.” Addressing reporters during a press conference at the Pentagon Tuesday morning, Hegseth said that “Iran, the cartels, Maduro, Yemen, every one was a lawful operation ordered by the Commander in Chief, then ordered by myself, notified to Congress, and executed by American warriors who did their jobs.”Even if the measure had passed the House, it was unlikely to obtain the two-thirds majority needed to pass the current Senate, where Republicans still hold 53 out ⁠of 100 seats. But that balance will change in the Democrats' favor next year.For now, Hegseth has the support of President Donald Trump, who vowed to “stand by” him even if an impeachment vote is successful, but the embattled Defense Secretary is facing mounting scrutiny elsewhere. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries was among those to throw his weight behind the impeachment effort. Jeffries is widely expected to be the new House Speaker come January, which would put him in a position of influence should another resolution be filed against Hegseth.While impeachment itself carries no immediate legal consequences, a conviction in the Senate can also result in disqualification from holding future federal office.“If you wanted to draw an analogy to criminal law: an impeachment vote by the House of Representatives is like an indictment. It doesn't mean the person has been found guilty, but it means that the House thinks there's enough evidence of high crime or misdemeanor that there should be a trial,” says Thomas Berry, director of the Cato Institute’s Center for Constitutional Studies.The House has initiated impeachment proceedings over 60 times, but only 22 cases, involving 21 people, have resulted in formal impeachment by the House. Trump was impeached twice by the House during his first term. He was accused of abusing the power of his office for domestic political advantage and obstructing Congress’ abilities to hold him accountable in the first impeachment, while the second impeachment saw him accused of incitement of insurrection, in relation to the events of Jan. 6, 2021. He was acquitted by the Senate in February 2020 and again in February 2021.If the House did vote to impeach Hegseth next year, he'd become the third Cabinet secretary to be impeached in U.S. history—here's what to know about the previous occasions, and how it played out. Secretary of War William W. Belknap is seen here —Heritage Art/Heritage Images—Getty ImagesHow William Belknap became the first Cabinet secretary to be impeachedWilliam Belknap served under Republican President Ulysses S. Grant from 1869 to 1876 as Secretary of War, a predecessor to the modern-day Secretary of Defense. (Although the Trump Administration has since revived the term after rebranding the “Department of Defense” as the “Department of War” last year.)Belknap, a Civil War veteran, came under scrutiny after Democrats regained the House majority in 1875 and began investigating the Grant Administration amid a series of scandals and allegations of financial corruption.“The Grant presidency was particularly corrupt. It was a situation where Grant himself was an honest man, a beloved war hero, turned two-term President,” says Thomas Balcerski, a professor of history at Eastern Connecticut State University. “Yet he had a flaw in his character in that he was too trusting of the men around him, many of whom were military figures from the Civil War.”In January 1876, the House passed a resolution directing committees with oversight of the executive branch to investigate government spending across all departments.The investigations turned to Belknap’s appointment of post-traders, civilian merchants licensed by the government to conduct business at military forts. These positions could be highly profitable, making the appointments a valuable source of patronage controlled by the secretary.Belknap was “accused of bribery, corruption, and taking kickbacks in exchange for essentially providing contracts,” says Balcerski. “These were basically kickback schemes. In the case of Belknap, he gave an exclusive contract, what we would call a ‘no-bid contract’ in our language today, specifically to trading posts in [modern day] Oklahoma.”While testifying in front of the Committee on Expenditures in the War Department, a wheeler-dealer named Caleb Marsh, who alongside Belknap handpicked associates to operate the lucrative military trading post at Fort Sill, alleged that Belknap had received payments in exchange for the appointments. Estimates placed the amount between $20,000 and $40,000, equivalent to approximately $630,000 to $1.26 million today.Belknap learned of Marsh’s testimony on March 1, 1876, and resigned the following day, just hours before the House unanimously voted to impeach him.His resignation, however, did not stop the impeachment proceedings from moving to the Senate, raising the constitutional question of whether an official could still face a trial after leaving office.“The only real dispute was whether the Senate could do anything about it, because Belknap had actually resigned hours before the House impeached him,” says Berry. “Much of the trial was not about whether he had been corrupt, but about whether the Senate could convict him, given the fact that he had already resigned.”Although the Senate could have voted to disqualify Belknap from holding future federal office, it ultimately did not reach the two-thirds majority necessary to convict him, and he was acquitted.Alejandro Mayorkas speaks at the White House on Oct. 1, 2024. —Kent Nishimura—Getty ImagesThe impeachment of Alejandro Mayorkas in 2024—and what came nextAlejandro Mayorkas served as Secretary of Homeland Security under former President Joe Biden from 2021 to 2025. He was impeached by House Republicans in 2024 over the Administration’s handling of the southern border, as federal officials during the Biden Administration had been overwhelmed by a surge in migrant crossings.The House of Representatives narrowly voted to impeach Mayorkas in February 2024. Republicans accused Mayorkas of failing to properly enforce the nation’s immigration laws.Balcerski says that, compared with Belknap, “there wasn't a similar signature scandal” surrounding Mayorkas’ impeachment. Instead, the case raised questions about the boundaries of impeachment and whether disagreements over how an official carries out government policy should constitute impeachable offenses.“That was pushing the boundaries of what is an impeachable offense,” argues Berry. “There has been much debate since the Constitution was ratified about what is a legitimately impeachable offense versus what is simply a disagreement in policy.”The Constitution identifies “conviction of, treason, bribery, or other high crimes and misdemeanors,” as grounds for removal from office, but the scope of what constitutes high crimes and misdemeanors lacks a formal definition, experts tell TIME.Ultimately, the Democrat-majority Senate dismissed Mayorkas’ articles of impeachment as unconstitutional in a single afternoon, two months after they were filed. Senate Democrats argued that allowing Cabinet officials to be impeached over disagreements with an Administration’s policies could set a dangerous precedent.The Biden Administration at the time denounced the move as “baseless” and "unconstitutional.” The DHS Office of the General Counsel also sent a 38-page response to the House Rules Committee, arguing that impeachment was being used to punish good-faith policy and enforcement decisions. Some Republicans raised doubts over the proceedings, also. Rep. Tom McClintock of California said that although he believed Mayorkas was “guilty of maladministration” of immigration laws, he did not view the matter as grounds for impeachment. “Many people thought that what Mayorkas had done did not rise to the level of a high crime or misdemeanor. That it was simply a political disagreement. That he was choosing to enforce immigration law with different priorities than a Republican DHS Secretary would, but that this was not objectively criminal or illegal,” says Berry.Mayorkas, who called the impeachment proceedings “baseless,” continued to lead the DHS until the transition to the second Trump Administration in January 2025.

items.title: Ex-member of radical Marxist group scales balcony, escapes house arrest in Argentina
items.standfirst: Leonardo Bertulazzi, 74, awaiting extradition to Italy, reportedly used harness to flee custodyA 74-year-old former member of Italy’s radical Marxist group the Red Brigades has escaped from house arrest in Argentina, the country’s security ministry confirmed on Wednesday, after he reportedly hid his ankle monitor inside a tube of pork and lowered himself from a fifth-floor balcony.Authorities placed Leonardo Bertulazzi under house arrest in Buenos Aires in 2024, prior to his extradition to Italy to serve a 27-year prison sentence. He had received the sentence in 1987 for joining a subversive association and belonging to an armed group. Continue reading...
